lesson.title: Angles in triangles and with parallel lines

widget.instructions: Drag corner B or use the slider to change the angles.

steps.text: Change the angle at A: the angle at B changes too, because the three angles of a triangle always add to 180°.
Here C is 90°, so A + B = 90°.
When a line crosses two parallel lines, alternate angles (a Z shape) are equal and co-interior angles (a C shape) add to 180°.
Tear off the three corners of any triangle and put them side by side: they make a straight line, 180°.
That is why the third angle is 180° minus the other two.

recap.text: Recap: triangle angles add to 180°; alternate angles are equal.

accessibility.altText: A right triangle whose angle can be changed.
accessibility.nonDragAlternative: Use the angle slider and the buttons; the description gives every angle.

steps.text: The area between a graph and the x-axis often means something: under a speed–time graph it is the distance.
Under a sloping straight line from x = 1 to x = 4 the region is a trapezium.
Its area is ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × width = ½ × (2 + 5) × 3 = 10.5.
Watch the area sweep out as x grows.
Split the trapezium into a rectangle under the lower height…
…plus a triangle on top: 3 × 2 + ½ × 3 × 3 = 10.5, the same answer.

recap.text: Recap: area under a straight line = trapezium ½(y₁ + y₂) × width, or rectangle + triangle.

lesson.title: Circle measurement: arc length and area

widget.instructions: Drag points or sliders where you see them; the description below names every value.

steps.text: This circle has radius 4. Its circumference is 2πr ≈ 25.1.
An angle at the centre measured in radians gives the arc length directly: s = rθ. A quarter turn is π/2 rad, so the arc is 4 × π/2 ≈ 6.28.
Degrees must be converted: θ (rad) = θ (deg) × π ÷ 180.
The area inside is πr² ≈ 50.3 square units.
Roll the circle along a line: one turn covers 2πr, the circumference.
A fraction of a turn covers the same fraction of 2πr: that is s = rθ.

recap.text: Recap: C = 2πr, s = rθ (θ in radians), A = πr².

accessibility.altText: A circle of radius 4 on a grid.
accessibility.nonDragAlternative: The graph is for reference; the steps describe every quantity.

lesson.title: The coordinate plane: distance and midpoint

widget.instructions: Drag points or sliders where you see them; the description below names every value.

steps.text: Every point is an (x, y) pair: P is at (1, 1) and Q at (4, 5).
Draw the right triangle between them: across 3, up 4.
The distance PQ is the hypotenuse: √(3² + 4²) = 5.
The midpoint averages the coordinates: ((1 + 4)/2, (1 + 5)/2) = (2.5, 3).
Drag P: the gaps Δx and Δy change, and so does the distance √(Δx² + Δy²).
The midpoint is always halfway in x and halfway in y.

recap.text: Recap: distance √(Δx² + Δy²); midpoint ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).

accessibility.altText: Two points on a grid joined by a line.
accessibility.nonDragAlternative: Drag point P or use its arrow keys; the description gives every coordinate.

widget.instructions: Change a force with Precise controls and press Play to see the motion it predicts.

steps.text: A force is a push or a pull with a size and a direction. Here the weight and the normal force balance.
The push is unbalanced, so the puck accelerates. Press Play.
Remove the push and the puck would keep its velocity: no force is needed just to keep moving.
Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the pull of gravity on it, mg (N).
Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced: the velocity changes in the direction of the net force.
A bigger unbalanced force gives a bigger acceleration.

recap.text: Recap: unbalanced force → acceleration; balanced → constant velocity; weight = mg.

accessibility.altText: A puck on ice with its weight, the normal force and a push.

lesson.title: Number systems on the number line

widget.instructions: Drag the ends of a piece, or use the buttons below the line.

steps.text: Every real number has a place on the number line. Integers sit at the whole-number marks.
Rational numbers are fractions p ÷ q of integers, like ½ or −3/4: they fill in between the integers.
Some numbers, like √2 ≈ 1.414…, can't be written as a fraction: they are irrational, but they still have a place on the line.
Distance on the line is always positive: from −3 to 2 is 2 − (−3) = 5.
Think of a number as a walk from 0: positive steps go right, negative steps go left.
The distance between two numbers is how far you walk from one to the other, whatever the direction.

recap.text: Recap: integers, rationals (fractions) and irrationals (like √2) all sit on the real number line; distance = larger − smaller.

accessibility.nonDragAlternative: Use the buttons below the number line; the description below it gives every position.

widget.instructions: Drag corner B or use the slider to change the angles.

steps.text: In a right triangle the side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse, always the longest.
Pythagoras: hypotenuse² = (one side)² + (other side)². Here 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5².
To find a shorter side, subtract: b² = c² − a².
Imagine a square on each side: the area of the big square equals the two small ones together.
Change the angle: the sides change, but a² + b² always equals c².

recap.text: Recap: c² = a² + b²; the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.

accessibility.altText: A right triangle with its side lengths.

steps.text: The roots of x² − 5x + 6 = 0 are where the parabola crosses the x-axis.
Factorise: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). A product is zero only when one factor is, so x = 2 or x = 3.
The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you how many roots there are: here 25 − 24 = 1 > 0, two roots.
Raise c: when D becomes negative the parabola no longer reaches the axis.
Any quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0 has x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ (2a).

recap.text: Recap: roots are x-intercepts; factorise or use the formula; D = b² − 4ac counts them.

steps.text: To solve 3x + 4 = 19, find where the line y = 3x + 4 meets y = 19.
Algebra does the same thing: undo each operation, doing the same to both sides. First subtract 4: 3x = 15.
Then divide both sides by 3: x = 5. The graphs meet at x = 5.
Formulas rearrange the same way: v = u + at becomes at = v − u, then a = (v − u) ÷ t.
Think of the equation as a balance: whatever you do to one side you must do to the other to keep it level.
Take 4 from each side, then share each side into 3 equal parts.

recap.text: Recap: undo operations in reverse order, doing the same to both sides.

lesson.title: Slope as a rate of change

widget.instructions: Drag points or sliders where you see them; the description below names every value.

steps.text: This line rises 1 unit for every 1 unit across: its slope is 1.
Slope = rise ÷ run, the change in y divided by the change in x.
Make the slope 2: the line rises twice as fast.
A negative slope falls from left to right. Steepness is the size of the slope, |m|.
On a distance–time graph, slope is speed: metres gained per second.
A steeper line means a faster rate of change.

recap.text: Recap: slope = rise ÷ run = Δy ÷ Δx; its sign gives the direction and its size the steepness.

accessibility.altText: A straight line whose slope can be changed with a slider.
accessibility.nonDragAlternative: Use the sliders or their arrow keys; the description below the graph gives every value.

widget.instructions: Change a lane's speed with its controls, then press Play.

steps.text: Speed tells you how many metres are covered each second. Press Play: the cyclist covers more metres every second.
Distance = speed × time: after 4 s the cyclist at 5 m/s has gone 20 m.
Rearranged: speed = distance ÷ time, and time = distance ÷ speed. Check the units: m ÷ (m/s) = s.

args.text: d = v t, v = d ÷ t, t = d ÷ v

steps.text: Cover the quantity you want: d on top, v and t below.
Covering t leaves d over v: time = distance ÷ speed. Press Play and read when the walker reaches 6 m.

recap.text: Recap: d = v × t; v = d ÷ t; t = d ÷ v. Keep the units consistent.

accessibility.altText: Two lanes: a walker and a cyclist moving at steady speeds.
accessibility.nonDragAlternative: Type speeds in the lane controls and press Play; the description gives every position.

steps.text: With a hypotenuse of 1, the opposite side is sin θ and the adjacent side is cos θ.
Pythagoras then says sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, for every angle.
At 30°: sin = ½, cos = √3/2. At 45°: both 1/√2. At 60°: sin = √3/2, cos = ½.
So if you know sin θ for an acute angle, cos θ = √(1 − sin²θ).
Cut an equilateral triangle of side 2 in half: the sides are 1, √3 and 2, with angles 30°, 60°, 90°.
Read the ratios from these sides: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2.

recap.text: Recap: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; sin 30° = ½, sin 45° = 1/√2, sin 60° = √3/2.

accessibility.altText: A right triangle with hypotenuse 1 and its sine and cosine shown.
accessibility.nonDragAlternative: Use the angle slider and the Mark θ buttons; the description gives every ratio.

lesson.title: Trigonometric ratios in a right triangle

widget.instructions: Drag corner B (or use the slider) to change the angle, and mark θ at A or B to see which sides are opposite and adjacent.

steps.text: This is a right triangle with the right angle at C. The longest side, AB, is across from the right angle: it is always the **hypotenuse**.
θ is the angle at A. The side across from θ is **opposite**. The other side that touches θ is **adjacent**.
Now move θ to corner B. Watch the labels: opposite and adjacent swap places, while the hypotenuse stays the same.
Back at A, the ratios: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. Watch them change as θ sweeps.
Your turn: drag corner B or use the slider, and mark θ at A or at B. Say which side is adjacent before you look at the labels.

args.text: Your turn: mark θ, then name the sides.

widget.instructions: A lamp shines straight down and straight across. Drag the vector's tip (or use the slider) and watch its shadows on the axes.

steps.text: Here is a vector of length r at θ above the x-axis. Its shadow on the x-axis (lamp overhead) and on the y-axis (lamp to the side) are its two components.
The x-shadow touches the angle θ at the origin: it is **adjacent**. So x = r cos θ.
The y-shadow sits across from θ: it is **opposite**. So y = r sin θ. Sweep θ and watch the two shadows trade length.

recap.text: Recap: the hypotenuse is across from the right angle, the opposite side is across from θ, and the adjacent side touches θ. sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent.

accessibility.altText: A right triangle ABC with the right angle at C and the angle θ marked at A. Each side is labelled opposite, adjacent or hypotenuse.
accessibility.nonDragAlternative: Use the angle slider and the Mark θ at A or Mark θ at B buttons; the description below the figure names each side.

widget.instructions: Press Play: the bars show the energy changing form.

steps.text: Work is done when a force moves something along its direction: W = F × d, measured in joules.
Energy is the ability to do work. A raised object has potential energy; a moving one has kinetic energy.
As the pendulum swings down, potential energy becomes kinetic energy; on the way up it changes back.
Without friction the total stays the same: energy changes form but is not used up.
A dropped ball loses height and gains speed: potential energy becomes kinetic energy.
Just before landing almost all the energy is kinetic.

recap.text: Recap: W = F d; PE ↔ KE; total energy is conserved.

accessibility.altText: A pendulum with kinetic and potential energy bars.
accessibility.nonDragAlternative: Use Play and the time slider; the description gives each energy.

widget.instructions: Step through the explanation, then press Play to see what the forces do to the sliding box.

steps.text: A box slides to the right after a push has ended. Before drawing any arrow, ask: what is pushing or pulling, and is it touching the box?
Gravity acts without touching: the Earth pulls the box down with its weight.
The floor touches the box: it pushes up (the normal force) and rubs against the sliding box (friction, backwards).
Nothing else touches the box, so there is no 'force of motion'. It keeps moving by inertia while friction slows it. Press Play.

accessibility.altText: A box sliding right on a floor. Forces are added one at a time: weight, normal force and friction.
accessibility.nonDragAlternative: Step through with Next; the description below the board lists each force and its agent.

widget.instructions: Step through the explanation; tick Tilted axes at any time to compare the two sets of axes.

steps.text: A block rests on a 30° slope. Its weight points straight down, but on a slope only two directions matter: along the slope and across it.
Turn the axes so that one runs along the slope and the other straight out of it.
Now the weight re-projects onto the new axes: mg sin θ along the slope and mg cos θ into it.
The plank pushes back only against the part pressing into it, so the normal force is mg cos θ, not mg.

accessibility.altText: A block on a slope at 30° with its weight drawn straight down.
